Pharyngealized vowels are phonemically distinct from non-pharyngealized vowels. new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Wangka dialect (Riung/Rembong-Riung) word stress generally falls on the second syllable of the word; since roots are overwhelmingly disyllabic this amounts to final-syllable stress in most words (the acute accents Rosen writes in the text, e.g. nange', ta.u', wali', pa.i', weto'n, diku', all sit on the second = last syllable). Rosen adds that stress is 'phonemic' (contrastive for some words) and marks it only sporadically.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is called 'phonemic, but not significant for all words', implying some lexical exceptions to the second-syllable tendency (none listed). Pharyngealized (per Schmidt: glottalized) vowels can also signal emphasis/stress on a word (na- vs na 'that').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in transcription notes to a narrative text recorded in Wangka village, Dec. 1975; hedged ('in general... tends to'). Not an analysis of phrase-level prominence; Rosen 1983:53 separately uses 'stress' for emphatic prominence of a word.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Rosen 1977) describes the speech of Wangka village (Riung district, Ngada), which Rosen calls 'the Riung language'; Glottolog files Wangka under remb1250 'Rembong-Wangka' (Schmidt 2014 and Asplund 2020 treat Wangka as a dialect of Rembong-Riung/Rembong-Wangka). Glottolog also has a separate languoid riun1237 'Riung' [riu]; Rosen's data are specifically Wangka, so remb1250 is the right key, but the statement should be tagged 'Wangka dialect'. Rembong proper (Elar, East Manggarai; Verheijen's dictionaries) is a different dialect cluster of the same language and is not covered by the quote.

sources.note: p.38: 'Stress is phonemic, but is not significant for all words... In general stress tends to fall on the second syllable of a word.' Also: pharyngealization of a vowel 'may be used to indicate stress' (na- 'that' vs na). Acute accents in the text (nange', ta.u', wali', zea', pa.i', weto'n, diku', aka'k) sit on the second = final syllable of disyllables.

sources.note: No Rembong-specific stress statement; Rembong appears in sound-correspondence tables and a note on /z/ (citing Verheijen 1977: vi). General areal remark only: 'While penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages, words with penultimate schwa can have stress on other syllables.'

sources.note: No word-stress rule. p.53: 'The pharyngealized vowel in Wangka is phonemic, but sometimes only occurs for the purpose of stress' (i.e. emphasis: a speaker 'wishes to stress the word'); Rembong has frequent post-vocalic glottal stops. Otherwise vocabulary/syntax comparison.
